interactions.label: Which of the following best describes the governing principle for ordering a sur

params.question: Which of the following best describes the governing principle for ordering a surgical investigation?

answers.text: A test should be ordered whenever a differential diagnosis has not been fully excluded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ordering tests to exclude every possibility leads to the cascade effect — incidental findings trigger more tests, biopsies, and sometimes unnecessary operations, causing real patient harm.

answers.text: A test should be ordered only if its result will change the management plan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. If the result will not alter what you do next, the test should not be ordered. This single question guards against both over-investigation and under-investigation.

answers.text: A test should be ordered to provide medicolegal documentation of a normal baseline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Establishing a baseline is one of four legitimate reasons to test, but only when that baseline is needed for clinical decision-making — not for routine documentation in every patient.

answers.text: A test should be ordered whenever the patient or family requests reassurance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Patient reassurance is important, but ordering investigations without a clinical question exposes the patient to unnecessary risks including radiation, contrast reactions, and the cascade of incidental findings.

overallFeedback.feedback: The governing principle is: will this result change what I do? If not, that test should not be ordered. The four legitimate reasons to investigate — confirm or exclude a diagnosis, define disease extent, establish a baseline, and assess surgical fitness — all derive from this single question.

Exactly right. The single governing discipline is: will this result change what I do? The four legitimate reasons — confirm or exclude a diagnosis, define disease extent, establish a pre-treatment baseline, and assess fitness for surgery — all flow from this principle.

params.question: A 50-year-old asymptomatic man has a mildly raised CA 19-9 on a routine health check. Why should this result NOT prompt a cancer work-up?

answers.text: CA 19-9 has very high specificity, so a mild rise is always a false positive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CA 19-9 does not have high specificity — it can be raised in benign biliary obstruction, pancreatitis, and other non-malignant conditions. The issue is not specificity alone but the inappropriate use of a monitoring marker for screening.

answers.text: Tumour markers are designed for monitoring known cancers and detecting recurrence, not for screening asymptomatic individuals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tumour markers like CA 19-9, CEA, and AFP are validated for tracking treatment response and recurrence in patients whose cancer already secretes that marker. Used as a screening test in a well person, a mildly raised value triggers a harmful investigation cascade.

answers.text: CA 19-9 is only elevated in biliary cancers and has no association with pancreatic malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CA 19-9 is in fact one of the markers associated with pancreatic cancer. The problem here is not the marker's organ association but its misuse as a screening tool in a patient without symptoms.

answers.text: A single mildly raised tumour marker always returns to normal on repeat testing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is not reliably true. A mildly raised CA 19-9 may persist due to benign causes. The fundamental issue is that tumour markers should not be used for screening — their role is monitoring treatment response and recurrence.

overallFeedback.feedback: Tumour markers like CA 19-9, CEA, and AFP are designed for monitoring known cancers, not for screening the well. A mildly raised marker in an asymptomatic person does not warrant a cancer work-up — it was the wrong test for the wrong question.

Well done. Tumour markers serve to monitor treatment response and detect recurrence in known cancers. Ordering them as screening tests in asymptomatic patients, as in the opening case, leads to unnecessary investigations without clinical benefit.

interactions.label: What is the key distinction between cancer screening and early diagnosis?

params.question: What is the key distinction between cancer screening and early diagnosis?

answers.text: Screening uses imaging modalities while early diagnosis relies on laboratory tests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both screening and early diagnosis may use any investigation modality — imaging, laboratory tests, or tissue sampling. The distinction lies in the target population, not the tool.

answers.text: Screening targets asymptomatic individuals before warning signs appear, while early diagnosis means prompt investigation of those who already have symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Screening tests people with no symptoms, aiming to find disease in its pre-clinical detectable phase. Early diagnosis acts on warning signs in a symptomatic person. Both exploit the same biological window but target different populations.

answers.text: Screening is applicable only to cancers with a known hereditary basis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Screening programmes exist for cancers without a primary hereditary basis — for example, cervical cancer screening with Pap smear and HPV testing. The criterion is a recognisable latent stage and an effective test, not a genetic link.

answers.text: Early diagnosis and screening are two names for the same public health strategy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: They are distinct strategies. A patient with rectal bleeding needs diagnostic work-up (early diagnosis), not a screening test. Screening statistics apply only to asymptomatic populations.

overallFeedback.feedback: Screening targets people without symptoms, aiming to detect disease in its pre-clinical phase. Early diagnosis means acting promptly on warning signs in a symptomatic patient. Both exploit the same biological window but target different populations and require different approaches.

Exactly. Screening targets the asymptomatic; early diagnosis targets the symptomatic. Both exploit the biological window between the onset of detectable disease and advanced cancer, but they address different populations with different tools.

interactions.label: Which of the following provides the strongest evidence that a cancer screening p

params.question: Which of the following provides the strongest evidence that a cancer screening programme is genuinely effective?

answers.text: The programme detects a larger number of cancers than were found before screening began

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Finding more cancers may reflect overdiagnosis — detecting indolent lesions that would never have caused harm. More diagnoses alone do not prove that the programme prevents death.

answers.text: Survival time from diagnosis is longer in screened patients than in unscreened patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lead-time bias inflates survival figures: diagnosis is simply made earlier without necessarily changing the date of death. A useless programme can appear successful by this measure.

answers.text: Cancer-specific mortality is reduced in the screened population compared to an unscreened control group

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Reduced mortality is the gold standard for evaluating a screening programme. Unlike survival time or detection rate, mortality reduction is not confounded by lead-time bias or overdiagnosis.

answers.text: The proportion of cancers diagnosed at an early stage increases after screening is introduced

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stage shift alone is necessary but not sufficient. Overdiagnosis of indolent early-stage lesions can inflate the early-stage proportion without actually reducing deaths from the cancer.

overallFeedback.feedback: The strongest evidence is reduced cancer-specific mortality in the screened population. Lead-time bias makes survival time unreliable — diagnosis is simply earlier without changing the outcome. Overdiagnosis inflates detection numbers. Only mortality reduction resists both biases.

Well reasoned. A sound screening programme is justified by reduced mortality in the screened population, not by finding more cancers or showing longer survival from diagnosis. Lead-time bias and overdiagnosis can make an ineffective programme appear successful by those other measures.
